claims.text: seed oils are bad for you

cited.title: Concerns about the health effects of industrially produced seed oils are without scientific foundation: a scoping narrative review of the clinical and observational evidence.
Perspective on the health effects of unsaturated fatty acids and commonly consumed plant oils high in unsaturated fat.

claims.explanation: Two reviews of human trials and observational studies looked specifically at whether seed oils and linoleic acid cause harm. They found that eating more of them goes with lower cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes risk and better blood fats, and that it does not raise markers of inflammation or oxidative stress. The scoping review concludes that worries about harm from seed oils, including from how they are made, have no scientific basis.
limitations: Both deciding papers are narrative or scoping reviews, not systematic reviews with meta-analysis
"Bad for you" is vague; the evidence covers mainly heart disease, diabetes, inflammation and oxidation, not every possible health outcome
The other retrieved papers are about industrial, chemical or skin uses of vegetable oils and do not test the claim

claims.text: saturated fats, which are totally fine

cited.title: Overfeeding polyunsaturated and saturated fat causes distinct effects on liver and visceral fat accumulation in humans.
Saturated fatty acids and total and CVD mortality in Norway: a prospective cohort study with up to 45 years of follow-up.
Saturated Fatty Acids and Cardiovascular Disease: Replacements for Saturated Fat to Reduce Cardiovascular Risk.
Erythrocyte saturated fatty acids and systemic inflammation in adults.
Saturated fatty acids are not off the hook.

claims.explanation: In a randomised trial, overeating saturated fat raised liver fat and visceral fat much more than overeating polyunsaturated fat (ev_24550191). A large Norwegian study that followed about 79,000 adults for up to 45 years linked higher saturated fat intake to higher death rates overall and from heart disease (ev_39279644). A review concluded that replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fats or whole grains lowers heart disease risk (ev_28635680), so the claim that saturated fats are "totally fine" does not hold. Only one review, focused on dairy (ev_36285545), found no clear link to heart disease, and it does not say saturated fats are harmless overall.
limitations: The mortality and inflammation findings come from observational studies, which show associations rather than proof of cause
The trial tested overeating saturated fat (palm oil) for 7 weeks, not normal intake
Some reviews suggest effects differ by food source (dairy versus others), and the evidence on heart disease is still debated

cited.title: Perspective on the health effects of unsaturated fatty acids and commonly consumed plant oils high in unsaturated fat.

claims.explanation: Reviews and a meta-analysis of trials report that swapping saturated fat for unsaturated plant oils improves cardiovascular risk factors such as LDL cholesterol, and that it is linked to lower cardiovascular and diabetes risk. However, the recovered Minnesota Coronary Experiment trial and its meta-analysis of five trials found that replacing saturated fat with linoleic-acid-rich oil lowered cholesterol but did not reduce coronary or all-cause deaths. That undercuts the claim that people are healthier "in almost every study".
limitations: The supporting reviews are narrative reviews and mostly report risk factors or observational links, not hard health outcomes.
The coconut oil meta-analysis compares oils on blood fats only; it only indirectly tests replacing saturated fat with seed oils.
The Minnesota trial took place in institutions in 1968–73 and used corn oil, so it may not reflect today's diets.
No paper measures the 'almost every study' frequency or general health months later.

gold_claims.notes: Good studies point in different directions. The 2020 Cochrane review finds reducing saturated fat cuts combined cardiovascular events by 21% (moderate quality) though with little or no effect on all-cause or cardiovascular mortality; a 2025 meta-analysis of nine trials finds no significant difference in any of those outcomes and concludes that saturated fat reduction cannot currently be recommended. Exactly the case MIXED exists for.

'Almost every study' overstates a split literature, which is why this is MIXED rather than SUPPORTED.

v23.gold_notes: @abbeyskitchen on the BBC World Service report into Steven Bartlett's Diary of a CEO podcast. Structurally unusual and useful for the stance step: the video opens cold on a clip of someone else's claims, with no framing until several seconds later, so a system reading only the first lines would see vaccine-autism and anti-COVID-vaccine assertions presented flat. The framing that makes it REFUTES arrives afterwards. All three refuted claims are contradicted by retrievable evidence, so DEBUNKING rests on solid ground. claims.text: [Gluten] can cause everything from osteoporosis to autism.
claims.explanation: One registry cohort found that people with celiac disease have more osteoporosis and fractures. That is an association limited to people with celiac disease, not proof that gluten causes osteoporosis in general. A small study found more anti-gliadin antibodies in some autistic children, but it shows an immune reaction in children who already have autism, not that gluten causes autism. Neither paper tests whether gluten causes these conditions in the general population.
limitations: Osteoporosis evidence covers only people with celiac disease, and it shows association, not cause
Autism study is small and cross-sectional; it measures immune reactivity in children who already have autism
No study tests whether gluten causes either condition in the general population

claims.text: The COVID vaccine introduction has had a catastrophic negative effect.
claims.explanation: None of the retrieved items measures the overall population-level effect of introducing COVID vaccines, so none tests whether it was "catastrophic". One item reports that a self-amplifying RNA vaccine had safety and efficacy comparable to BNT162b2 in trials. Another is a single case report of panuveitis after an mRNA vaccine. Most of the other items are titles only, with no abstract.
limitations: Most items have titles only, with no abstracts to assess
No population-level study of vaccine harms against benefits was retrieved
The claim is vague: 'catastrophic negative effect' is not defined
The case report and the trial summary are only indirect evidence

limitations: The retrieved evidence is off-topic: it is about paediatric quality-of-life instruments, not podcast misinformation.
The BBC analysis cited in the claim was not retrieved, so the figures could not be checked against it.

claims.text: anti-vaccine conspiracies
claims.explanation: The claim, "anti-vaccine conspiracies", names a topic but does not say anything that could be true or false, so no evidence can test it. The retrieved papers describe anti-vaccine conspiracy talk (an editorial, and an analysis of posts on a white nationalist forum about COVID-19). Neither tests a specific health or safety statement.

The evidence consists of an editorial and an analysis of online discussion, not studies of health outcomes

claims.text: [proven cancer treatments are] toxic

cited.title: Strategies to mitigate the toxicity of cancer therapeutics.
New methods in the diagnosis of cancer and gene therapy of cancer based on nanoparticles.
Tumor inflammation-associated neurotoxicity.

claims.explanation: Several reviews say standard cancer treatments cause toxicity. These include chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted drugs, immunotherapy, radiation and cell therapies. Reported harms include nerve damage (neuropathy), gut, kidney and hearing damage, and treatment-specific neurotoxicity, partly because these treatments can kill healthy cells as well as cancer cells. These are recognised side effects that doctors manage. The papers do not say the treatments are unusable or that the harms outweigh the benefits.
limitations: All the evidence is narrative reviews, not systematic quantification of harms
How toxic a treatment is varies widely by type, dose and patient; some treatments, such as surgery for thyroid cancer, are not described mainly in terms of toxicity
The papers present toxicity as a side effect that can be managed, set against proven benefit; they give no basis for avoiding treatment

claims.text: you can reverse autism through diet
claims.explanation: The only dietary study is an uncontrolled pilot of 7 children with autism on a ketogenic diet for 4 months. It reported changes in inflammation markers and gut bacteria, and an earlier report on the same group found better sociability, but it does not show that autism was reversed. None of the other papers test diet, and none find against the claim, so MIXED does not apply.
limitations: The ketogenic diet pilot had only 7 children, no control group and no randomisation
Better symptoms or biomarkers are not the same as reversing autism
The other retrieved papers are reviews or studies on unrelated autism topics (vaccines, brain structure, diagnosis)

gold_claims.text: The COVID vaccine introduction has had a catastrophic negative effect
gold_claims.notes: The global estimate finds more than 2.5 million deaths averted by COVID-19 vaccination over 2020-2024 (one death averted per 5400 doses), with sensitivity analyses between 1.4 and 4.0 million lives saved. A net catastrophic negative effect is the opposite of that.

gold_claims.text: you can reverse autism through diet
gold_claims.notes: The systematic review of six randomised trials (214 participants) of gluten- and casein-free diets finds no statistically significant differences in autism core symptoms between groups, with one exception on a single communication subdomain. That refutes reversal through diet; medium confidence because the trials test one dietary approach rather than every possible one.

claims.text: seed oils are unhealthy, leads to inflammation, heart disease, obesity
claims.explanation: Neither retrieved paper looks at seed oils as normally eaten. One review covers industrial trans fats from partially hydrogenated oils and links them to inflammation and heart disease, but that is a processing product, not seed oils in general. The other covers phytosterols, which are plant compounds found in oils, mostly in mechanism studies, and says they lower LDL cholesterol.
limitations: The trans fat review is about partially hydrogenated oils, not unhydrogenated seed oils
The phytosterol review covers one component of oils and is mostly about mechanisms and preclinical work
No trials or cohort studies of seed oil intake and inflammation, heart disease or obesity were retrieved
Both papers are narrative reviews

claims.text: if you eat seed oils it leads to inflammation
claims.explanation: The only retrieved paper is a systematic review of functional foods in clinical trials. It lists flaxseed oil and grape seed oil among the foods reported to regulate inflammation, but it does not directly test whether eating seed oils in general, such as soybean, corn or sunflower oil, causes inflammation. None of the evidence tests the claim as stated.
limitations: The review covers functional foods broadly and does not focus on the omega-6-rich seed oils usually meant by 'seed oils'
The abstract only says these foods 'regulate' inflammation and gives no effect sizes or direction for each oil
No study looks at typical dietary seed-oil intake and inflammation markers

claims.text: carbs make you fat

cited.title: Association between changes in carbohydrate intake and long term weight changes: prospective cohort study.
Different carbohydrate exposures and weight gain-results from a pooled analysis of three population-based studies.

claims.explanation: A large US cohort (ev_37758268) linked more starch, added sugar, refined grains and starchy vegetables with more weight gain. In the same cohort, more carbs from whole grains, fruit and non-starchy vegetables went with less weight gain. A pooled Finnish cohort analysis (ev_37149710) found no link between total carbohydrate intake and weight gain, so the evidence suggests carb type matters, not carbs as a whole.
limitations: Both weight studies are observational and cannot show cause and effect
No randomised trials of carb intake vs. fat gain were retrieved
The claim is a blanket statement, while the evidence varies by carbohydrate type
The athletic-performance, mortality and diabetes papers do not address weight gain

claims.text: It is not carbs or fat that make you fat, it is how many calories you're eating.
claims.explanation: None of the retrieved papers directly compares diets with equal calories but different carb and fat content and measures fat gain. Most look at how carbohydrate affects athletic performance, or at mortality. One small trial found that pistachios led to more BMI loss than pretzels at similar calories, which hints that the food matters. But it is a single study of snack type, not a test of carbs versus fat versus calories.
limitations: Most papers are about sports performance, not body weight or fat gain
Pistachio RCT is small, tests one snack swap during calorie restriction, and only hints against the claim
No metabolic-ward trials or meta-analyses comparing equal-calorie diets with different carb and fat content were retrieved

claims.text: It might be easier to overeat processed carbs
claims.explanation: None of the retrieved papers looks at whether processed carbohydrates lead to overeating, energy intake or satiety. Most cover carbohydrates for athletic performance. The others cover carbohydrate intake and mortality, and carb counting for diabetes.
limitations: No studies on ultra-processed or refined carbohydrates and energy intake were retrieved
Most papers are about sports nutrition, a different topic
The mortality cohort study is observational and does not measure overeating

claims.text: if you're eating whole foods that contain lots of fiber and complex carbs, it's going to be harder to overeat those because they are more filling
claims.explanation: None of the retrieved papers measures satiety, fullness or energy intake after eating high-fiber whole foods, so none tests whether such foods are harder to overeat. The reviews link fiber and whole grains to heart and metabolic health, gut microbiota and lower body weight. Those are associations, not tests of the satiety mechanism the claim describes.
limitations: No study measures satiety, appetite or ad libitum energy intake
The weight link in ev_23609775 is observational and does not show that fiber makes food more filling
Two papers are about dairy cattle nutrition and are not relevant
Several items are only titles or broad narrative reviews

claims.text: Carbs are an essential part of your diet.
claims.explanation: None of the retrieved papers tests whether carbohydrates are an essential nutrient. A large cohort meta-analysis (ev_30122560) linked both very low and very high carbohydrate intake with higher death rates, but this is only an association. A trial in triathletes (ev_39786965) found that a very-low-carbohydrate diet still sustained endurance performance. The rest are reviews of how athletes use carbohydrate as fuel; none addresses whether carbs are needed in the diet at all.
limitations: Most papers are about athletes' performance, not about whether people in general need carbs in their diet
The mortality evidence is observational and shows only an association, and the results depended on what replaced the carbohydrate
No reference source on nutrient requirements (for example, dietary reference intakes) was retrieved

claims.text: The butter should be eaten as a snack and it is healthy for you to do so.

cited.title: Butter and Plant-Based Oils Intake and Mortality.
Butter, margarine and serum lipoproteins.

claims.explanation: A large US cohort of 221,000 adults followed for up to 33 years found that people who ate the most butter had 15% higher total mortality and higher cancer mortality, while swapping butter for plant oils was linked to lower mortality. A review of 20 diet trials found that replacing butter with soft margarine improved blood lipids. Neither study suggests that eating more butter is healthy.
limitations: No study tests butter eaten specifically as a snack; the evidence covers butter intake in general.
The mortality evidence is observational: it shows an association, not cause.
The lipid review compares butter with margarine and measures blood lipids, a stand-in for health outcomes.
The other retrieved items are letters, off-topic papers or have no abstracts.

claims.text: Saturated fats are fine to eat in moderation, especially if you're an active person with a generally healthy lifestyle.
claims.explanation: None of the retrieved studies tests whether moderate saturated fat intake is safe, and none looks at active people with healthy lifestyles. A large Norwegian cohort linked higher saturated fat intake (median about 15% of calories) to higher death rates, and an overfeeding trial found saturated fat increased liver and visceral fat. A narrative review argues that the link between saturated fat and heart disease is weaker than often assumed. These findings are indirect and point in different directions, so they cannot confirm or refute the claim as stated.
limitations: No study defines or tests 'moderate' intake, or looks specifically at active or healthy-lifestyle people
The harm signals come from observational associations (cohort, cross-sectional, biomarker studies) or from overfeeding, not normal intake
The supportive material is a narrative review and opinion pieces, mostly about dairy and heart disease

claims.text: it probably is not optimal to increase your intake to extreme amounts
claims.explanation: The claim doesn't say which nutrient it means or what counts as an "extreme" amount, so it can't be tested as stated. The one retrieved paper, a review of carbohydrate intake for athletes, recommends about 30–90 g per hour during long events. It does not look at whether intakes far beyond that are less than optimal or harmful.
limitations: The claim doesn't name the nutrient or define 'extreme', which leaves little to test
The only evidence is a narrative review of carbohydrate fuelling in athletes, which does not test very high intakes
Hedged wording ('probably not optimal') makes the claim hard to falsify

claims.text: You can gain fat in a calorie deficit due to hormonal problems or endocrine dysfunction.
claims.explanation: The only paper retrieved is a 1997 narrative review of how alcohol affects the endocrine system. It does not look at fat gain, energy balance or calorie deficits, so nothing here tests whether hormonal problems can cause fat gain during a calorie deficit.
limitations: The only paper is off-topic: it covers alcohol's effects on hormones, not fat gain during a calorie deficit
No studies measure body fat or energy balance in people with endocrine disorders
It is a narrative review, and an old one (1997)

claims.text: Fat gain or loss is still a function of how many calories you are eating and burning.
claims.explanation: Neither retrieved paper tests whether fat gain or loss is determined by calories eaten versus calories burned. One is a classroom laboratory exercise that teaches energy expenditure and fat oxidation and assumes the energy-balance principle. The other is a narrative review of adipocyte mitochondria that describes adipose tissue as central to energy balance but does not test the claim.
limitations: The lab exercise is a teaching activity that assumes energy balance; it does not test it in people
The mitochondria review is mechanistic and only indirectly related
No controlled feeding trials or authoritative reference on energy balance were retrieved

claims.text: vegetables are bad for you

cited.title: Vegetables, fruit, and cancer prevention: a review.
Fruit and vegetables in cancer prevention.
Fruits, vegetables, 100% juices, and cognitive function.

claims.explanation: Reviews of many human epidemiologic studies link higher vegetable and fruit intake with lower risk of several cancers, and the 1996 review also notes benefits for heart disease, stroke, diabetes and other conditions. A 2014 review found that most studies report cognitive benefits. None of the retrieved papers show that vegetables in general are harmful.
limitations: Most evidence is observational and narrative reviews; association does not prove cause
Studies often combine fruit and vegetables
The IARC-based review rates the evidence for cancer prevention as only limited
Several retrieved papers (microbiome, agriculture, consumer acceptance) do not address health effects

claims.text: Some vegetables do contain anti-nutrients that may bind up specific minerals and stop them from being absorbed

cited.title: Is There Such a Thing as "Anti-Nutrients"? A Narrative Review of Perceived Problematic Plant Compounds.

claims.explanation: The narrative review names plant compounds commonly called anti-nutrients, including oxalates, phytates and tannins, and examines whether they pose a real health threat. These are the compounds known to bind minerals, which fits the claim's modest wording that some vegetables contain compounds that "may" reduce mineral absorption.
limitations: Only one narrative review was retrieved, and only its abstract.
The abstract does not itself state that these compounds bind minerals or reduce their absorption.
The review questions how much these compounds matter for health, which the claim does not address.

claims.explanation: The claim doesn't say which food it means. None of the retrieved papers looks at whether eating a particular food gives a net gain in nutrients. Neither one looks at food variety itself, and the other three papers are about forests, fish and moths.
limitations: No study measures dietary diversity or food variety scores against health outcomes
The diet and fibre reviews are narrative reviews of observational cohort studies, and they address diet quality or fibre, not variety
Three of the retrieved papers have nothing to do with nutrition

v65.gold_notes: Dr. Rubin taking apart a viral 'things they told us were unhealthy' video point by point, and explaining the technique as he goes: flash a citation too briefly to read, take a kernel of truth, shroud it in things out of context. The salt segment is the best-documented example in the bundle of citation misuse -- he names the PURE study, the journal and the year, and then explains why spot urine sodium samples cannot carry the conclusion drawn from them. That is a methodological critique, not a contradiction, so the refuted claim lands on MIXED and the video comes out CANNOT_RECOGNIZE rather than DEBUNKING. Under the revised section 9 it now goes to review as a possible debunk of an unsettled claim, which is the outcome that rule was written for. Collectors filed it under DEBUNKING.

claims.text: doctors … lied to you about [salt] being unhealthy … physicians were withholding information on purpose for some type of secondary gain

cited.title: Dietary salt intake and cardiovascular outcomes: an umbrella review of meta-analyses and dose-response evidence.
The impact of excessive salt intake on human health.
Impact of Salt Intake on the Pathogenesis and Treatment of Hypertension.
Sodium.
Salt: a narrative review and local policy initiatives in Israel.

claims.explanation: The claim depends on the advice that "salt is unhealthy" being a lie, and the evidence shows that advice is accurate. Several reviews agree. Whether doctors held back information on purpose for gain cannot be tested by these papers, but medical advice that matches the evidence is not a lie.
limitations: No paper looks at what doctors intended or whether they had something to gain; that part of the claim cannot be tested here
The evidence is about excessive salt; some studies suggest very low intake may also carry risk, and that remains debated
